Boss
BAWS
adjective (Boomer slang)
Two unrelated words share the spelling. The noun boss, a master or employer, is American from the seventeenth century, from Dutch baas (master) in New Amsterdam. The adjective boss, "excellent, first-rate," grew out of it: it is recorded in nineteenth-century American slang and was revived in the 1950s–60s among Black and teenage speakers ("that car is boss"); Los Angeles station KHJ branded itself "Boss Radio" in 1965. The 1828 boss — a stud or knob, from French bosse — is a third, older word (see bosses).

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In Boomer slang, boss means excellent, the best, top of the heap: "That’s a boss Mustang." The word borrows the glory of the man in charge and pins it on whatever is admired. The Christian observation: the slang quietly assumes that being the boss is the highest thing — that to call something "boss" is to give it the top rank. The Lord Jesus turned that assumption over. When His disciples argued about who would be greatest, He said, "whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister; And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant: Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Mat 20:26–28). In His kingdom the boss is the one who serves. Paul tells earthly masters to remember that they too are under authority: "Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven" (Col 4:1). And the Lord says flatly, "one is your Master, even Christ" (Mat 23:10). So a Christian can enjoy the word — a car can be boss, a guitar riff can be boss — while teaching his children where true excellence lives. The truly boss thing in the universe is a King who washed His servants’ feet.

Webster 1828 Definition

Boomer slang (19th c., revived 1950s–60s) for excellent, first-rate, from boss (master) — a word that crowns being in charge, which Christ redefined: "whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant" (Mat 20:27).

BOSS, adj. (Boomer slang, 1950s–60s; earlier 19th-c. American) Excellent, outstanding, first-rate. "That’s a boss car." "Boss Radio." From boss, n., a master or employer (Dutch baas).

Note: the 1828 boss (a knob or stud) is a different word from French bosse, a swelling — see bosses (Job 15:26).

Decode for families: Gen Z’s nearest equivalents are fire, goated, elite.

Key Scripture

Mat 20:26 — "But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;"

Mat 20:27 — "And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant:"

Mat 20:28 — "Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."

Col 4:1 — "Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven."

Mat 23:10 — "Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, even Christ."

Modern Corruption

The slang crowns whatever is admired with the title of the man in charge; Christ crowns the servant, and reminds every master that he has a Master in heaven.

expand to see more

Language reveals what a culture admires, and boss reveals a lot. The best thing you can say about a car or a song is that it is like the man who gives orders. That is the world’s ranking, and the disciples shared it until the night before the cross, when they were still arguing about rank at the Lord’s Supper. The gospel does not abolish authority — masters and servants, parents and children, elders and congregations all remain — but it relocates greatness. The greatest in the kingdom is the one who serves (Mat 20:26).

For a father, the word is an opportunity. In your household you are, in a real sense, the boss. Scripture asks you to be the kind of boss Col 4:1 describes — just and equal, knowing you answer to a Master in heaven — and the kind Mat 20:28 embodies, giving yourself for those under you. A son who sees that will learn what boss really means.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Dutch baas (master) → American boss (17th c.) → adj. boss (excellent, 19th c.; revived 1950s–60s); distinct from 1828 boss (knob, French bosse).
